title: Revisiting Simple Baselines for Relational Deep Learning

paper.title: Revisiting Simple Baselines for Relational Deep Learning
paper.abstract: Abstract Relational deep learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning end-to-end predictive models over relational databases by representing them as temporal heterogeneous graphs. Recent advances based on graph neural networks and Transformers have achieved strong performance across diverse domains. However, the effectiveness of simpler relational baselines remains underexplored, making it difficult to assess how much architectural complexity is needed to achieve strong predictive performance. Motivated by the observation that predictive signals arise from target attributes, relational attributes, and historical labels, we revisit how effectively these signals can be exploited using simple propagation methods. We adapt fixed low-pass feature propagation to relational entity graphs and train an MLP for prediction. The resulting predictions are further refined using Correct-and-Smooth, a graph-based label propagation algorithm that incorporates historical labels over task-specific meta-graphs connecting target entities. Across classification and regression tasks on RelBench, an MLP trained on neighborhood-filtered features outperforms one using only target-entity features on most tasks and recovers a substantial portion of the performance of heterogeneous GNNs. Correct-and-Smooth provides further gains from historical labels, although applying it requires a separately constructed meta-graph because connections among target entities are not directly specified by the relational entity graph. Together, our studies revisit the effectiveness of established propagation methods as simple RDL baselines while identifying canonical meta-graph construction as a key challenge for effective label propagation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Example of graph conversion. (Left) A relational entity graph, where each node is an entity, and edges are primary–foreign key links. (Right) All nodes are collapsed into a single type, and feature sets are merged and normalized. Data in domains such as e-commerce, healthcare, and social media is predominantly stored in relational databases, where tables are linked through primary–foreign key relationships. To reduce feature engineering efforts, relational deep learning (RDL) provides a framework for predictive modeling directly over such databases by representing each table row as a node in a temporal heterogeneous graph, whose edges encode primary–foreign key relationships [ 1 , 2 ] . This representation enables graph neural networks (GNNs) and transformer-based models to aggregate information across related entities, and has established RDL as an effective paradigm for learning on large-scale relational databases [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Early approaches primarily adapted heterogeneous GNNs with relation-aware message passing to relational databases [ 2 , 4 , 3 ] . Recent advances adopted transformer-based architectures with the aim of building relational foundation models, which achieved strong performance on large-scale benchmarks [ 8 , 6 ] . In parallel, closed-source relational foundation models demonstrated that large-scale pretraining produces representations that transfer across databases and tasks [ 5 , 7 ] . Across these models, the predictive signal on an entity-level task can be grouped into three sources: the attributes of the target entity, the attributes of entities related to it through foreign keys, and the historical labels of the target and of related entities. These models utilize target and relational attributes by sampling a temporal neighborhood around each target entity and aggregating its features through GNN message passing [ 2 , 4 ] or Transformer attention [ 8 , 6 ] . Recent work further shows that historical labels can add substantial predictive signals to improve zero-shot predictions [ 6 ] . Simple counterparts for exploiting these three sources are well established in graph learning. Specifically, an MLP operates directly on node features, fixed neighborhood propagation incorporates information from neighboring nodes without learned message passing [ 9 ] , and Correct-and-Smooth ( C&S ) propagates label information over a graph [ 10 ] . However, these methods are typically studied on homogeneous static graphs and cannot be applied to relational entity graphs directly. RDL graphs are heterogeneous, with nodes from different tables carrying different feature spaces. Additionally, they are temporal, requiring propagation to respect the time of each prediction, and labels are available only for the target entities of a task, rather than for all nodes in the graph. In particular, the graph induced by the database schema is not necessarily an appropriate graph for propagating task labels. In this work, we make three contributions. First, we adapt established propagation methods to a simple RDL baseline that separates the three sources of predictive signal. We train an MLP on target attributes, then train the same MLP architecture on features enriched by fixed relational propagation [ 9 ] , before refining its predictions with historical labels through the post-processing step with C&S [ 10 ] . Second, we evaluate how much performance these stages recover on RelBench [ 11 , 12 ] : feature propagation improves over the unfiltered MLP on 20 of 21 tasks and brings average classification AUROC within two points of the supervised heterogeneous GNN baseline. Finally, we study task-specific meta-graphs for label propagation and highlight canonical, temporally valid graph construction as a key challenge for exploiting historical labels in RDL.

sections.heading: 2 Simple Propagation for Relational Deep Learning
sections.text: We describe how feature and label propagation incorporate the three sources of predictive signal into the baseline. Appendices B and C give the feature construction, filter definition, and C&S updates.

sections.heading: 2.1 Relational Entity Graphs
sections.text: A relational database induces an entity graph G = ( 𝒱 , ℰ ) G=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) , where nodes are table rows and edges represent primary–foreign key links [ 2 ] . Each row carries attributes and, when applicable, a timestamp. An entity-level task provides labeled examples ( e , t ) (e,t) , where e e is the target entity and t t is the seed time; predictions may use only information available by t t . While RDL models typically learn relation-specific aggregation on this graph [ 2 , 4 ] , we use it for fixed feature propagation before training an MLP.

sections.heading: Homogeneous relational graph
sections.text: We combine all primary–foreign key links into one adjacency matrix and place each table’s encoded attributes in a separate block of feature columns. This gives a homogeneous propagation graph while keeping attributes from different tables distinct (Figure 1 ). Appendix B describes the encoding and normalization.

sections.heading: Low-pass propagation with temporal visibility
sections.text: For each seed time t t , we remove rows with later timestamps, retain static rows, and apply a fixed low-pass filter [ 9 ] to the visible graph. Each propagation step combines a node’s features with those of its neighbors using symmetric degree normalization. We then train an MLP on the resulting representations, using K = 2 K=2 steps in the main experiments. The K = 0 K=0 baseline uses target attributes alone, with structural features disabled. More details on the filtering process and feature definitions are also provided in Appendix B .

sections.heading: 2.3 Label Propagation with Correct-and-Smooth
sections.text: After training on the filtered features, we incorporate historical labels through C&S [ 10 ] to refine the MLP predictions. In particular, the Correct stage propagates residuals from labeled nodes to adjust the MLP predictions, and the Smooth stage propagates these predictions with observed labels as anchors. Since task labels belong to target entities that may be connected only indirectly in the relational graph, we construct a separate meta-graph over their prediction rows and historical labels. We compare meta-graphs that attach the target’s own history and related entities’ labels directly or through temporal chains. Each construction admits only labels observed strictly before the seed time (Appendix C.1 ) with propagation settings selected on validation before refining the MLP predictions.

sections.heading: 3 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate whether the three simple propagation stages can provide a competitive relational baseline across the entity-level classification and regression tasks in RelBench-v1 [ 11 ] and RelBench-v2 [ 12 ] . We exclude rel-f1 and rel-event , for which temporal leakage has been reported [ 6 , 13 ] . Following RelBench, classification is evaluated using AUROC [ 14 ] and regression using MAE. Our experiments follow the three stages introduced in Section 2 . The unfiltered MLP uses only the attributes of the target entity and corresponds to K = 0 K=0 . The filtered MLP uses K = 2 K=2 steps of fixed feature propagation and therefore incorporates attributes from related entities. Finally, filtered MLP + C&S applies label propagation to the filtered predictions using the graph variant that incorporates both historical labels and neighboring labels ( Cross+Self ), which is described in Appendix C.1 . We select the C&S configuration on validation using the task metric (Appendix C ). All reported results are averaged over ten random seeds. Task statistics and training details are given in Appendices A and B . We compare our method against HeteroGNN , the supervised RelBench baselines [ 11 , 12 ] .

sections.heading: 4 Discussion
sections.text: In conclusion, we evaluate an MLP on target attributes, enrich its inputs through fixed feature propagation, and refine its predictions with historical labels through C&S . Our results show that fixed feature propagation recovers substantial relational signal without learned aggregation, providing a simple baseline for assessing the gains from more complex RDL models. However, historical labels pose a different challenge: the schema connects related entities but does not specify which connections support label propagation. The variation across meta-graphs therefore motivates task-aware constructions that capture useful label dependencies while respecting temporal visibility alongside more efficient preprocessing to reduce the cost of filtering each seed-time snapshot (Appendix B.2 ).

sections.heading: Appendix A Benchmark Tasks and Constructed Graphs
sections.text: This section describes how we build the homogeneous graph for feature filtering based on the database schema, and how the tasks in the datasets are defined with labels.

sections.heading: Databases.
sections.text: Each database is converted once into the collapsed graph and stacked feature matrix described in Section 2 , independently of the task evaluated on that database. Table 4 summarizes the resulting representations, reporting the number of graph rows, the dimensionality of the feature matrix, the distribution of this dimensionality across text, numerical, and other column types, and the number of parameters in the resulting MLP. In particular, feature dimensions and model sizes vary substantially across databases. For example, rel-avito has 622 622 input dimensions, while rel-trial has 15,145 15{,}145 , mainly from text, and an MLP roughly 24 × 24\times larger. This feature dimensionality, rather than the number of labeled examples, is the primary factor driving precomputation costs for some databases (Appendix B.2 ).

sections.heading: Tasks.
sections.text: Within each database, each task provides labeled examples, which RelBench splits into train, validation, and test sets according to the chronological order [ 11 ] . Table 3 reports the sizes of these splits together with the number of distinct seed times, which determines the number of filtered snapshots computed for each task. Tasks defined on the same database share the underlying graph but require separate snapshots. Consequently, tasks with more seed times incur higher precomputation costs. For example, hm / user-churn , with 54 54 seed times, requires substantially more snapshot computation than the avito tasks, which have 5 5 seed times. We evaluate all entity-level classification and regression tasks except those from rel-event , for which temporal leakage has been reported, and rel-f1 , which [ 13 ] identify as likely compromised. sections.heading: Appendix B Feature Propagation and Training Details
sections.text: In this section, we describe in detail how to encode and normalize attributes once per database, then append structural features for each visible snapshot.

sections.heading: Step 1: Column encoding.

Categorical columns use indicators for the six most frequent values and the log-frequency of the row’s value, counted through the validation timestamp. Other timestamp columns encode years relative to the row’s time, or since 1990 for tables without a time column. Concatenating the encodings of all non-key columns of T i T_{i} yields X i ∈ ℝ n i × d i X_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{i}\times d_{i}} , where n i = | T i | n_{i}=|T_{i}| and d i d_{i} denotes the encoded dimensionality of table T i T_{i} . Table 4 reports the resulting dimensions aggregated per database. Primary and foreign keys are excluded from the feature representation and are used solely to define the graph structure.

sections.text: The filter is precomputed per task: the collapsed graph and the stacked features are shared by all tasks of a database, but one snapshot is computed per distinct seed time of the task and read out at the task’s entity rows, so cost grows with the seed-time count of Table 3 . We measured the filtering time, ranging from 5.5 5.5 minutes ( rel-avito ) to 47 47 minutes ( rel-stack ) for one representative task per database; on rel-avito , deepening the filter to K = 10 K=10 grows this to 113 113 minutes. Dense design matrices dominate memory, requiring roughly ( rows ) × ( d + 2 ) × 4 (\text{rows})\times(d+2)\times 4 bytes per snapshot. Serial peak memory ranged from 44 44 GB ( rel-avito ) to 214 214 GB ( rel-amazon ). This process can be further sped up by utilizing GPUs for filtering, which remains as future work.

sections.heading: B.3 Training Details
sections.text: The prediction head follows the reference MLP of [ 10 ] , with batch normalization removed. It consists of a single hidden layer of width 256 256 , followed by ReLU activation and dropout with rate 0.5 0.5 . The same architecture is used across all datasets and is trained with Adam using a batch size of 512 512 , following RelBench configurations [ 11 ] . We remove batch normalization because its running statistics are estimated from the training period and can degrade substantially under RelBench’s temporal test shift. On one task, for example, removing batch normalization left validation AUROC unchanged but prevented test AUROC from collapsing from 0.886 0.886 to 0.224 0.224 . Then, we train with binary cross-entropy for classification and ℓ 1 \ell_{1} loss for regression, clipping regression predictions to the 2nd–98th percentile range of training targets [ 11 ] . Evaluation uses the official RelBench AUROC and MAE implementations, with MAE reported in the target’s original units. We select the learning rate on validation from { 10 − 3 , 3 ⋅ 10 − 3 , 10 − 2 } \{10^{-3},3{\cdot}10^{-3},10^{-2}\} and stop after 5 epochs without improvement in the validation metric. We use the official RelBench splits [ 11 , 12 ] without modification. The benchmark fixes validation and test timestamps per database, generates labeled examples at a calendar stride, and masks test labels; we do not perform any additional re-splitting. All results are averaged over ten fixed seeds. To reproduce our results, readers can select the following seeds: { 0 , 7 , 13 , 21 , 42 , 77 , 123 , 555 , 1234 , 2026 } \{0,7,13,21,42,77,123,555,1234,2026\} , which control MLP initialization and batch shuffling. The filter is deterministic on the relational entity graph. The baselines additionally employ per-edge-type message functions and column encoders on top of comparable input encoders, whereas our model uses a single prediction head after feature propagation. Thus, our prediction head has fewer trainable parameters by construction.

sections.heading: Comparison to the RDL training pipeline.
sections.text: RelBench-style models such as RelGNN and RelGT sample a temporal neighborhood for each labeled row, restrict it to information visible at the seed time, and jointly train the relational model and prediction head. Our pipeline instead filters the full visible graph once per seed time, then trains an MLP on the resulting rows. This moves relational computation into preprocessing, allowing the filtered features to be computed once and reused.

Each label is one hop away, but its edge weight decreases with age rank. For example, the newest label receives weight 1 1 , the next 0.7 0.7 , and so on. This construction uses the entity’s own past outcomes as context, with greater edge weight on recent observations. (b) Cross . We instead use the most recent label of each selected related entity, connecting it directly to the prediction row with its co-occurrence weight. The target’s own labels are omitted. This construction asks whether related entities provide useful label information, including when the target has no label history of its own. (c) Cross+Self . We attach both the target’s full label history and the newest label of each selected related entity directly to the prediction row. Both sources are therefore one hop away. Unlike Self , own-label edges here have weight 1 1 throughout, while related-label edges retain their co-occurrence weights. This is the construction used in the main results. (d) Cross+Hist . For each selected related entity, we insert an unlabeled relay between the prediction row and up to three of that entity’s newest labels. The relay includes the base prediction associated with its newest label, while its attached history nodes carry the observed labels. This gives each related entity a local history around an intermediate prediction node; label information reaches the target through two hops. The target’s own history is omitted. (e) All . We extend Cross+Hist with the target’s own history, also through relays. Each own past label creates a separate unlabeled relay carrying the base prediction associated with that label. Every own relay receives fresh copies of the same up to three newest own labels, and all edges in these own-history branches have weight 1 1 . Thus, the number of own relays follows the full history length, while each relay’s labeled neighborhood remains limited to three observations. (f) Self-Chain . We arrange the target’s full history along a path: the prediction row connects to the newest label, that label to the next newest, and so on. All edges have weight 1 1 , and related entities are omitted. Older observations lie progressively more hops from the prediction row, so the topology encodes recency instead of assigning a different edge weight to each past label. (g) Chain+Cross . We retain the own-history path of Self-Chain and add a direct edge to the newest label of each selected related entity, weighted by co-occurrence. Own and related histories therefore enter through different routes: older own labels lie along the temporal path, while each related entity contributes one label at one hop. (h) Chain+Hist-3 . We build a separate temporal path for the target and for each selected related entity, keeping up to three newest labels in every path, including the target’s. The first edge of a related path has its co-occurrence weight; all remaining edges, including the own-history path, have weight 1 1 . This construction represents recent histories from both sources through the same temporal ordering, without unlabeled relays. (i) Chain+Hist . We remove the three-label limit from Chain+Hist-3 and retain all visible labels in both the own and related histories. Each history still forms a newest-first path with the same edge-weight rules, placing older observations farther from the prediction row. Comparing these two variants therefore examines the effect of retaining longer histories under the same attachment rules.

There are three emerging patterns in the experiments. First, improvements are generally small and construction-dependent. Thus, no single construction consistently outperforms the others, and some constructions are detrimental. For example, the self-label star reduces AUROC by 2.7 2.7 points on avito / user-clicks . sections.heading: E.5 Discussion and Open Questions
sections.text: Overall, our studies show that simple propagation methods allow lightweight models to recover a substantial portion of relational predictive power without learned aggregation. Integrating historical label signals further improves performance on tasks where target entities carry informative past outcomes. Nevertheless, the relational database schema itself does not specify which entity connections support effective label propagation. Since shared records create structural links without guaranteeing correlated labels, establishing a canonical method of graph construction for label propagation remains essential for advancing relational deep learning under realistic temporal constraints.

Affiliation: Stanford University Email: gunther.gust@uni-wuerzburg.de Gunther Gust Affiliation: University of Würzburg Email: dwi@seamlesslabs.ai Abstract Relational deep learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning end-to-end predictive models over relational databases by representing them as temporal heterogeneous graphs. Recent advances based on graph neural networks and Transformers have achieved strong performance across diverse domains. However, the effectiveness of simpler relational baselines remains underexplored, making it difficult to assess how much architectural complexity is needed to achieve strong predictive performance. Motivated by the observation that predictive signals arise from target attributes, relational attributes, and historical labels, we revisit how effectively these signals can be exploited using simple propagation methods. We adapt fixed low-pass feature propagation to relational entity graphs and train an MLP for prediction. The resulting predictions are further refined using Correct-and-Smooth, a graph-based label propagation algorithm that incorporates historical labels over task-specific meta-graphs connecting target entities. Across classification and regression tasks on RelBench, an MLP trained on neighborhood-filtered features outperforms one using only target-entity features on most tasks and recovers a substantial portion of the performance of heterogeneous GNNs. Correct-and-Smooth provides further gains from historical labels, although applying it requires a separately constructed meta-graph because connections among target entities are not directly specified by the relational entity graph. Together, our studies revisit the effectiveness of established propagation methods as simple RDL baselines while identifying canonical meta-graph construction as a key challenge for effective label propagation. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Example of graph conversion. (Left) A relational entity graph, where each node is an entity, and edges are primary–foreign key links. (Right) All nodes are collapsed into a single type, and feature sets are merged and normalized. Data in domains such as e-commerce, healthcare, and social media is predominantly stored in relational databases, where tables are linked through primary–foreign key relationships. To reduce feature engineering efforts, relational deep learning (RDL) provides a framework for predictive modeling directly over such databases by representing each table row as a node in a temporal heterogeneous graph, whose edges encode primary–foreign key relationships [ 1 , 2 ] . This representation enables graph neural networks (GNNs) and transformer-based models to aggregate information across related entities, and has established RDL as an effective paradigm for learning on large-scale relational databases [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Early approaches primarily adapted heterogeneous GNNs with relation-aware message passing to relational databases [ 2 , 4 , 3 ] . Recent advances adopted transformer-based architectures with the aim of building relational foundation models, which achieved strong performance on large-scale benchmarks [ 8 , 6 ] . In parallel, closed-source relational foundation models demonstrated that large-scale pretraining produces representations that transfer across databases and tasks [ 5 , 7 ] . Across these models, the predictive signal on an entity-level task can be grouped into three sources: the attributes of the target entity, the attributes of entities related to it through foreign keys, and the historical labels of the target and of related entities. These models utilize target and relational attributes by sampling a temporal neighborhood around each target entity and aggregating its features through GNN message passing [ 2 , 4 ] or Transformer attention [ 8 , 6 ] . Recent work further shows that historical labels can add substantial predictive signals to improve zero-shot predictions [ 6 ] . Simple counterparts for exploiting these three sources are well established in graph learning. Specifically, an MLP operates directly on node features, fixed neighborhood propagation incorporates information from neighboring nodes without learned message passing [ 9 ] , and Correct-and-Smooth ( C&S ) propagates label information over a graph [ 10 ] . However, these methods are typically studied on homogeneous static graphs and cannot be applied to relational entity graphs directly. RDL graphs are heterogeneous, with nodes from different tables carrying different feature spaces. Additionally, they are temporal, requiring propagation to respect the time of each prediction, and labels are available only for the target entities of a task, rather than for all nodes in the graph. In particular, the graph induced by the database schema is not necessarily an appropriate graph for propagating task labels. In this work, we make three contributions. First, we adapt established propagation methods to a simple RDL baseline that separates the three sources of predictive signal. We train an MLP on target attributes, then train the same MLP architecture on features enriched by fixed relational propagation [ 9 ] , before refining its predictions with historical labels through the post-processing step with C&S [ 10 ] . Second, we evaluate how much performance these stages recover on RelBench [ 11 , 12 ] : feature propagation improves over the unfiltered MLP on 20 of 21 tasks and brings average classification AUROC within two points of the supervised heterogeneous GNN baseline. Finally, we study task-specific meta-graphs for label propagation and highlight canonical, temporally valid graph construction as a key challenge for exploiting historical labels in RDL. 2 Simple Propagation for Relational Deep Learning We describe how feature and label propagation incorporate the three sources of predictive signal into the baseline. Appendices B and C give the feature construction, filter definition, and C&S updates. 2.1 Relational Entity Graphs A relational database induces an entity graph G = ( 𝒱 , ℰ ) G=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) , where nodes are table rows and edges represent primary–foreign key links [ 2 ] . Each row carries attributes and, when applicable, a timestamp. An entity-level task provides labeled examples ( e , t ) (e,t) , where e e is the target entity and t t is the seed time; predictions may use only information available by t t . While RDL models typically learn relation-specific aggregation on this graph [ 2 , 4 ] , we use it for fixed feature propagation before training an MLP. 2.2 Feature Propagation Homogeneous relational graph We combine all primary–foreign key links into one adjacency matrix and place each table’s encoded attributes in a separate block of feature columns. This gives a homogeneous propagation graph while keeping attributes from different tables distinct (Figure 1 ). Appendix B describes the encoding and normalization. Low-pass propagation with temporal visibility For each seed time t t , we remove rows with later timestamps, retain static rows, and apply a fixed low-pass filter [ 9 ] to the visible graph. Each propagation step combines a node’s features with those of its neighbors using symmetric degree normalization. We then train an MLP on the resulting representations, using K = 2 K=2 steps in the main experiments. The K = 0 K=0 baseline uses target attributes alone, with structural features disabled. More details on the filtering process and feature definitions are also provided in Appendix B . 2.3 Label Propagation with Correct-and-Smooth After training on the filtered features, we incorporate historical labels through C&S [ 10 ] to refine the MLP predictions. In particular, the Correct stage propagates residuals from labeled nodes to adjust the MLP predictions, and the Smooth stage propagates these predictions with observed labels as anchors. Since task labels belong to target entities that may be connected only indirectly in the relational graph, we construct a separate meta-graph over their prediction rows and historical labels. We compare meta-graphs that attach the target’s own history and related entities’ labels directly or through temporal chains. Each construction admits only labels observed strictly before the seed time (Appendix C.1 ) with propagation settings selected on validation before refining the MLP predictions. 3 Experiments We evaluate whether the three simple propagation stages can provide a competitive relational baseline across the entity-level classification and regression tasks in RelBench-v1 [ 11 ] and RelBench-v2 [ 12 ] . We exclude rel-f1 and rel-event , for which temporal leakage has been reported [ 6 , 13 ] . Following RelBench, classification is evaluated using AUROC [ 14 ] and regression using MAE. Our experiments follow the three stages introduced in Section 2 . The unfiltered MLP uses only the attributes of the target entity and corresponds to K = 0 K=0 . The filtered MLP uses K = 2 K=2 steps of fixed feature propagation and therefore incorporates attributes from related entities. Finally, filtered MLP + C&S applies label propagation to the filtered predictions using the graph variant that incorporates both historical labels and neighboring labels ( Cross+Self ), which is described in Appendix C.1 . We select the C&S configuration on validation using the task metric (Appendix C ). All reported results are averaged over ten random seeds. Our results show that fixed feature propagation recovers substantial relational signal without learned aggregation, providing a simple baseline for assessing the gains from more complex RDL models. However, historical labels pose a different challenge: the schema connects related entities but does not specify which connections support label propagation. The variation across meta-graphs therefore motivates task-aware constructions that capture useful label dependencies while respecting temporal visibility alongside more efficient preprocessing to reduce the cost of filtering each seed-time snapshot (Appendix B.2 ). It consists of a single hidden layer of width 256 256 , followed by ReLU activation and dropout with rate 0.5 0.5 . The same architecture is used across all datasets and is trained with Adam using a batch size of 512 512 , following RelBench configurations [ 11 ] . We remove batch normalization because its running statistics are estimated from the training period and can degrade substantially under RelBench’s temporal test shift. On one task, for example, removing batch normalization left validation AUROC unchanged but prevented test AUROC from collapsing from 0.886 0.886 to 0.224 0.224 . Then, we train with binary cross-entropy for classification and ℓ 1 \ell_{1} loss for regression, clipping regression predictions to the 2nd–98th percentile range of training targets [ 11 ] . Evaluation uses the official RelBench AUROC and MAE implementations, with MAE reported in the target’s original units. We select the learning rate on validation from { 10 − 3 , 3 ⋅ 10 − 3 , 10 − 2 } \{10^{-3},3{\cdot}10^{-3},10^{-2}\} and stop after 5 epochs without improvement in the validation metric. We use the official RelBench splits [ 11 , 12 ] without modification. The benchmark fixes validation and test timestamps per database, generates labeled examples at a calendar stride, and masks test labels; we do not perform any additional re-splitting. The baselines additionally employ per-edge-type message functions and column encoders on top of comparable input encoders, whereas our model uses a single prediction head after feature propagation. Thus, our prediction head has fewer trainable parameters by construction. Comparison to the RDL training pipeline. RelBench-style models such as RelGNN and RelGT sample a temporal neighborhood for each labeled row, restrict it to information visible at the seed time, and jointly train the relational model and prediction head. Our pipeline instead filters the full visible graph once per seed time, then trains an MLP on the resulting rows. This moves relational computation into preprocessing, allowing the filtered features to be computed once and reused. Reproducibility.
